subject: physics
title: Stopping distance and reaction time
key_idea: **Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.** Thinking distance is the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time. Braking distance is the distance travelled while the brakes slow the vehicle. Each factor changes one or both distances.

sections.heading: Thinking distance, braking distance and stopping distance

blocks.text: This section explains how a vehicle stops in an emergency and which distances are involved.

items.meaning: The time between a driver seeing a hazard and starting to brake.
The distance the vehicle travels during the driver's reaction time.
The distance the vehicle travels under the braking force, until it stops.
The total distance the vehicle travels from the hazard being seen to the vehicle stopping.

blocks.label: Stopping distance
blocks.formula: stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance
where: stopping distance, thinking distance and braking distance are all in metres, m

items: During the thinking distance the vehicle keeps moving at the same speed.
During the braking distance the brakes slow the vehicle down.
For a given braking force, the greater the speed, the greater the stopping distance.
Stopping distance is the sum of thinking distance and braking distance.
The driver controls the thinking distance. The brakes, tyres and road control the braking distance.
A greater speed gives a greater stopping distance.

blocks.text: Reaction times vary from person to person. Typical values range from 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
A longer reaction time means the vehicle travels further before the driver starts to brake. This increases the thinking distance.
What changes a driver's reaction time

items: Tiredness.
Drugs.
Alcohol.
Distractions, such as using a mobile phone.

blocks.label: Thinking distance
where: distance is the thinking distance, in metres, m
speed is the speed of the vehicle, in metres per second, m/s
time is the reaction time, in seconds, s

diagram.alt: Calculate a thinking distance from a speed and a reaction time.
diagram.question: A car travels at {v} m/s. The driver's reaction time is {t} s. Calculate the thinking distance.

items: A simple method is for one student to drop a ruler and another to catch it. The distance the ruler falls before it is caught shows the reaction time: a longer distance means a longer reaction time.
Repeat the test several times and take a mean to reduce the effect of chance.
Compare the results with and without a distraction to see its effect on reaction time.
Reaction time is typically 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
Tiredness, drugs, alcohol and distractions increase reaction time.
A longer reaction time gives a longer thinking distance, not a longer braking distance.

blocks.text: Braking distance depends on the vehicle, the road and the weather. It does not depend on the driver's reaction time.

items: Wet or icy roads reduce the friction between the tyres and the road.
Poor tyres, such as worn tyres, reduce the friction between the tyres and the road.
Poor brakes, such as worn brakes, reduce the braking force.
A greater mass means more kinetic energy to remove, so the braking distance is greater.
A greater speed means more kinetic energy to remove, so the braking distance is greater.

blocks.text: Try the slider. Change the speed, the driver and the road, and watch which distance changes.

diagram.alt: Set the speed, the driver and the road to see the thinking, braking and stopping distances.

items: The driver changes the thinking distance only.
The road, tyres and brakes change the braking distance only.
Speed changes both distances.
You may be asked to estimate how the stopping distance of a vehicle changes over a range of typical speeds.
(Separate science) You may be asked to interpret graphs of speed against stopping distance for a range of vehicles.
Leave a bigger gap to the vehicle in front on wet or icy roads.
Keep tyres and brakes in good condition.
Do not drive when tired or after drinking alcohol or taking drugs.
Do not use a mobile phone while driving.
Friction between tyres and road, brake condition and mass change the braking distance.
Road, tyre and brake conditions do not change the thinking distance.
In an answer, link each factor to the distance it changes, with a reason.

checks.q: State the equation for stopping distance.
checks.a: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

checks.q: Explain why a person should not drink alcohol and then drive.
checks.a: Alcohol increases reaction time, so the thinking distance increases. The driver is more likely to have a collision before stopping.

checks.q: A car travels at 20 m/s. The thinking distance is 14 m. Calculate the driver's reaction time.
checks.a: Reaction time = thinking distance ÷ speed = 14 ÷ 20 = 0.70 s.

worked_example.question:
The stopping distance of a car is the sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance.

Explain why a person should not drink alcohol and then drive.
answer_points: So the thinking distance increases (the car travels a greater distance).
So the driver is more likely to have a collision before stopping in an emergency.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each linked step: reaction time, thinking distance, then the risk of a collision.

worked_example.question:
The driver's reaction time is the time between the driver seeing an emergency and starting to brake.

A car is travelling at a speed of 31 m/s.

The car travels 46 m between the driver seeing an emergency and starting to brake.

Calculate the driver's reaction time.

Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
worked_example.tip: One mark for substitution, one for the evaluation and one for giving 2 significant figures.

worked_example.question:
The table shows thinking, braking and stopping distances for the same car travelling at different speeds.

Speed (m/s) | Thinking distance (m) | Braking distance (m) | Stopping distance (m)
8 | 6 | 6 | 12
16 | 12 | 24 | 36
32 | 24 | 96 | 120

Calculate the reaction time of the person driving the car.
worked_example.tip: A correct answer of 0.75 s scores all 3 marks. A correct substitution is ignored if it is not rearranged.

worked_example.question:
The speed of a car affects the thinking distance and the braking distance.

Discuss other factors that affect the thinking distance and the braking distance of the car.
answer_points: Up to two factors that change the thinking distance: tiredness of the driver, age of the driver, alcohol or drugs, or a distraction such as a mobile phone.
Up to two factors that change the braking distance: mass of the car, condition of the brakes, condition of the road (icy or wet), condition of the tyres, or the slope of the road.
worked_example.tip: Each factor scores a mark, up to two for thinking distance and two for braking distance.
